item.title: Inside the Nepal Tunnel Rescue Operation
item.description:
When the Australian geologist and engineer Arnold Dix was approached by the Nepal authorities to help find those who could be trapped in hydropower project tunnels after a major flood last week, he knew there were several pressing challenges.

First, rescuers needed to locate the projects and their entrances, because everything had been “removed” by the force of the flood, Mr. Dix said.

“It took us the better part of a day or two, just to figure out where the power stations used to be and also to develop a plan as to how might we save people if they survived,” he said.

Hundreds of workers have been missing in the tunnels since last Wednesday, when a glacial collapse sent tsunami-like waves of water mixed with rock and debris through two river valleys, killing more than 1,300 people and leaving more than 4,000 missing in Nepal and neighboring China.

Nepal has built a robust hydroelectric industry, harnessing the fast-flowing waters in the Himalayas to generate electricity. Those projects require both manual and engineering work to construct tunnel systems deep into the earth. Many hydropower projects have been constructed along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli Rivers, which bore the brunt of the flooding.

Mr. Dix and his team’s efforts were focused on the Trishuli 3A hydropower project.

Mr. Dix’s team relied on engineering drawings of the structures underground, satellite imagery and old charts to try and identify any potential “Goldilocks zones” — a term Mr. Dix used to describe a small subterranean area “where a human being could have survived.”

This information would guide rescuers on where to start looking. Most of their efforts have been focused in the project’s cable tunnel — which runs from the underground powerhouse to the transmission grid, he said.

Mr. Dix is now en route to Kathmandu from Australia to help with rescue efforts on the ground. He has advised on major underground rescue operations around the world, including a tunnel collapse in the Himalayas three years ago, when 41 workers were rescued after being trapped for 17 days.

This operation has been slow and difficult work, he said. Rescuers have had to dig through mud and use explosives to blast through rocks “the size of cars.” Once inside the tunnel, they were faced with water that needed to be drained, he added.

“We had to dig a huge drainage canal back to the river — the new river which is now not where it used to be — because we were worried that the tunnel was full of water, and it would drown us, or maybe drown people who were ahead of us in the tunnel,” Mr. Dix said.

Rescuers then were able to create a small gap along the top of the cable tunnel through which they could crawl, calling to any survivors.

Those immense efforts paid off on Friday.

Mr. Dix said rescuers heard the “faint sound of someone in Nepalese acknowledging” their calls.

A short time later, at least two workers were found alive. They have been flown to Kathmandu for treatment. One is in a critical condition.

One of the rescued, Sanjay Sah, is a mechanical foreman and the other, Kabir Maharjan, is a mechanical supervisor, according to a list seen by The New York Times. Both were employees of the Nepal Electricity Authority, according to the list.

More than 40 people were thought to be inside the tunnel, according to two people briefed on the rescue operations, including a senior Nepali Army officer. Rescuers also heard other voices in the tunnel, the people said, kindling hope that more people could be saved. It was not clear how many were still alive.

“I was in tears, of course,” Mr. Dix said of the moment he found out the good news.

For both survivors, challenges remain, he said. “They don’t know what’s happened; they’ve been cut off from the world the whole time, they’ve been trapped in the dark for more than a week,” he said.

“They’re going to find out that thousands of people have died, including their friends and colleagues,” he added.

There will be no rest for Mr. Dix. Once he arrives in Kathmandu on Friday evening, he will put what he has learned from this rescue “into strategies about how we might go and help other power stations.”

He said the efforts of the rescue team were extraordinary, adding, “we’re performing miracles out there.”

Anupreeta Das contributed reporting.

item.title: U.N. Approves African Proposal for a New World Map
item.description:
The United Nations General Assembly on Friday endorsed a world map that depicts the size of Africa more accurately than the map most commonly used now.

The assembly approved a resolution favoring the Equal Earth projection, a map that supporters say shows the true size of countries, over the familiar Mercator map, which shrinks regions near the Equator. It passed with 164 votes in favor and six abstentions, according to Reuters. The only nation that voted against the resolution was the United States, which said the map promoted an “ideological agenda” and was a distraction from the “genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations,” Reuters reported.

The new map has supporters in Africa, who say the Mercator projection has contributed to a historical bias that has minimized tropical and equatorial regions and exaggerated the size of countries near the poles.

The U.N. resolution does not outlaw the Mercator projection or require the use of the Equal Earth map. But it is part of a campaign to raise awareness of the effects of visual representations of the Earth on how people view the world.

Here’s what to know about the debate.

The projection, one of many ways to represent the spherical Earth on a flat plane, was designed by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate.

It was created by projecting the Earth’s features onto a cylinder, then flattening that into a rectangle.

The map was invaluable for seafaring: Any straight line drawn on the map represents a compass direction that sailors can use to determine which way to go. The projection has since become widely used in books, classrooms and online services like Google Maps.

Every map projection makes sacrifices, like shape, size or distance: You can’t flatten a round object without somehow stretching, shrinking or tearing it. The Mercator projection reflects true directions but distorts the size of landmasses.

If you had a Mercator projection on your classroom wall, you might have grown up believing that Greenland, for example, is as big as Africa, even though it is one-14th its size. You might also think that Alaska is bigger than Mexico, when it is 25 percent smaller.

Critics have argued that the Mercator map creates a subtle bias whereby northern nations, including some of the world’s wealthiest, appear large and equatorial regions, home mostly to developing countries, are depicted as small. Some cartographers say it reinforces a Eurocentric and colonial worldview.

The Equal Earth projection — created in 2018 by the cartographers Bojan Savric, Bernhard Jenny and Tom Patterson — sacrifices straight-line directions in order to render landmasses in their correct proportions. It has rounded edges to account for the Earth’s spherical shape instead of a rectangle.

Advocacy groups in Africa have campaigned to replace the Mercator map since April 2025. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August that year, urging its 55 member states to adopt the Equal Earth map in schools and public communications. The West African nation of Togo sponsored the U.N. resolution, backed by other countries in the African Union.

“A map is never neutral,” Robert Dussey, the foreign minister of Togo, said on Thursday, promoting the U.N. resolution. “It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood and may, sometimes from the earliest years of schooling, perpetuate representations that do not correspond to geographic reality.”

The resolution before the U.N. General Assembly calls on the more than 190 member states to update their educational materials and educate students about the accurate sizes of countries and the limitations of different map projections.

It also urges major digital map providers to discuss the issue with governments and adopt more accurate cartographic representations.

The resolution is not binding. But the push to replace the Mercator map has made progress in other ways.

Google, which used a Mercator-based map for more than a decade, shifted in 2018 to showing the Earth as a globe when zoomed out on the desktop platform. “Greenland’s projection is no longer the size of Africa,” the company said on social media.

Some schools have begun replacing Mercator maps. Boston Public Schools in 2017 began purchasing maps with the Peters projection, which shows countries in their correct proportional sizes to one another at the cost of stretching and squashing their outlines.

The shift was part of the district’s effort to “decolonize the curriculum,” Colin Rose, then a district administrator, told The Boston Globe.

item.title: Philippines’ Vice President Faces Arrest Over Assassination Threats
item.description:
A Philippine court on Friday ordered the arrest of the country’s vice president, Sara Duterte, over charges that she threatened to have President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., the first lady and a former speaker of the House of Representatives assassinated.

It was the latest turn in the acrimonious, yearslong feud between Ms. Duterte and Mr. Marcos, former allies who are scions of two Philippine political dynasties.

The charges stem from a late-night news conference Ms. Duterte gave nearly two years ago, when she was being investigated for corruption. In the speech, she said that she had made arrangements for Mr. Marcos, his wife, Liza; and Martin Romualdez, the president’s cousin and the speaker at the time, to be assassinated if she were killed.

It was not the first time Ms. Duterte had spoken of violence against Mr. Marcos — a few weeks earlier she had threatened to behead him. But it elicited a response from the president, who did not name the vice president but spoke of “criminal intent.”

Last month, the Philippine Department of Justice filed a criminal case against Ms. Duterte. On Friday, a regional court in Quezon City issued a warrant on three counts of making “grave threats.” The court set bail at 120,000 pesos, about $1,900, for each count, which Ms. Duterte posted on Saturday morning, her lawyer Paul Lim told reporters. Her booking procedures were briefly delayed after Ms. Duterte refused to enter the court without her supporters, saying that she feared for her life and wanted witnesses present.

Ms. Duterte has said her comments about Mr. Marcos and his family were “maliciously taken out of logical context.” Her allies have argued that she cannot be criminally prosecuted while she is in office.

“Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” Mr. Lim said in a statement on Friday.

Around five years ago, Mr. Marcos and Ms. Duterte formed an unlikely alliance that propelled them to the two highest positions in the country. But their partnership collapsed quickly after the election, with both camps hurling accusations of corruption against the other.

The acrimony spiraled further last year, when Mr. Marcos facilitated the arrest of his predecessor, Rodrigo Duterte, who is Ms. Duterte’s father. He is facing charges at the International Criminal Court of crimes against humanity over his brutal antidrug campaign.

Ms. Duterte has faced other legal issues. She has been impeached twice and is currently facing trial in the Philippine Senate. A conviction would bar her from holding public office. But she remains the leading contender for president in the next election, which is scheduled for 2028.

item.title: 9 Days After Flood, 2 Men Are Pulled Alive From Mud-Filled Tunnels in Nepal
item.description:
The rescuers heard voices. They crawled through a sludge-filled tunnel deep underground where employees of a hydroelectric plant in Nepal had been trapped for nine days.

“We are coming!” Lt. Col. Ganga Baral, one of the leaders of the operation, said he had called out. “Don’t worry, the Nepali Army is coming.”

On Friday morning, two mud-caked survivors were rescued from the tunnels and hoisted into the open air, an extraordinary moment captured on video and in photos by the army.

The improbable rescue provided a measure of hope a week and a half after a glacial collapse unleashed a tsunami of mud and boulders that killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left thousands of others missing.

The men were rescued from a hydroelectric center buried so deeply in the detritus of the flood that engineers had to use satellite images to pinpoint its location amid the disfigured landscape.

Hirashova Maharjan, the wife of Kabir Maharjan, one of the workers rescued, described her husband as deeply disoriented after being airlifted to Kathmandu, the capital, for medical treatment.

“He didn’t even recognize me,” she said from the army hospital in Kathmandu. But his condition has since improved, she said.

“He is stable now,” she said. “We’re so happy. We are crying with happiness. Thank you to the army and to the government.”

The raging floodwaters that erupted on Aug. 26 washed away roads, bridges and, in some cases, entire villages.

The two men were rescued from a tunnel in the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project. The body of a third man, a mechanical engineer, was also recovered on Friday, according to Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha, the head of the Nepal Electricity Authority.

More than 40 other workers were thought to be inside the tunnel, according to Sanjay Sah, one of the rescued men. It was not clear how many were still alive.

Mr. Sah was able to answer questions through an oxygen mask. He spoke from a stretcher in a video that was posted to a government ministry’s Facebook page. He said he thought three or four people were still alive in the area where he had been found.

“I used to work in the control room as an operator,” he says in the video. “Usually there would be four or five people there, but at the time, there were 40 or 45.”

He added: “I tried to get everyone out and tried to warn everyone. But then I ran out of time.”

Mr. Sah, who was a mechanical foreman at the hydroelectric plant, said he had recited prayers “over and over again” during his time trapped underground in darkness. “How many days has it been?” he asked.

The rescue efforts have been grueling. Images posted by the Nepali Army showed rescuers slithering through sludge deep in the tunnels with hard hats and flashlights. Other rescuers paddled through tunnels in inflatable dinghies, the kind used in white-water rafting.

Arnold Dix, an Australian geologist and engineer who is assisting the Nepalese authorities in the rescue operations, said it had taken a day or two to locate the power stations and to develop a plan to rescue the workers.

Nepal has a large hydroelectric industry that harnesses the fast-flowing waters in the Himalayas. Many of the projects have tunnel systems deep in the earth along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, which bore the brunt of the flooding.

Mr. Dix said he had focused on the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, relying on engineering drawings of the structures underground, satellite imagery and old charts to try and identify any potential “Goldilocks zones” — a term he used to describe a small subterranean area “where a human being could have survived.”

Most of the rescue efforts have been focused in the project’s cable tunnel, which runs from the underground powerhouse to the transmission grid.

The operation has been slow and difficult work, Mr. Dix said. Rescuers have had to dig through mud and use explosives to blast through rocks “the size of cars.” Once inside the tunnel, they were faced with water that had to be drained, he added.

Workers had to dig a huge drainage canal back to the river.

“We were worried that the tunnel was full of water, and it would drown us, or maybe drown people who were ahead of us in the tunnel,” Mr. Dix said.

Rescuers were then able to create a small gap along the top of the cable tunnel through which they could crawl, calling to any survivors. That was the area where rescuers found Mr. Maharjan and Mr. Sah.

Mr. Sah’s family had all but given up hope that he might be found alive. Dev Sah, his brother- in-law, said that the family had decided just a day earlier to provide a DNA sample in case his body needed to be identified.

On Friday, Dev Sah said he had spoken to the rescued man at the hospital and had to reassure him repeatedly that he was now safe.

“He has received a new life today,” Dev Sah said.

Mujib Mashal, Alex Travelli and Binod Ghimire contributed reporting.

item.title: Kenyans Did College Students’ Homework For Years. Then A.I. Arrived.
item.description:
Teresios Bundi once symbolized the strange, life-changing opportunities the internet provided.

Hailing from a farming village in Kenya, Mr. Bundi moved to the capital, Nairobi, in 2011 to be the first in his family to attend university. There, a friend suggested he try a new online job: writing essays for cheating overseas college students.

His first assignment was a two-page essay on the health benefits of the Garcinia cambogia. It was a fruit he had never heard of, and an essay written for a student he didn’t know anything about. He earned $7 for three hours of work.

“That was a lifeline for me, I needed the money,” Mr. Bundi, now 34, said in an interview in Nairobi. He added: “I could not sleep that night. I was ready to burn the midnight oil.”

Mr. Bundi estimates he wrote more than 2,500 essays over the next 12 years, sometimes three a day. He balanced completing his public health degree with helping faraway students studying engineering, medicine and computer science to finish theirs. Some students gave him their school login information so he could keep up with their assignments.

Mr. Bundi didn’t know it then, but he was in the boom era of internet gig work. Newly wired to the global internet and hungry for jobs, well-educated youths from places like Kenya, the Philippines and India found opportunities in the crevices of the digital economy. They could make money online doing unglamorous tasks that others further up the economic ladder did not want to do.

Then A.I arrived, and the good times ended.

In 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT. At colleges worldwide, students made a simple calculation that has become more pronounced today: Why pay a freelancer in Kenya when ChatGPT could do the job?

Essay work began to thin. Rates fell, and assignments dwindled. Before long, the industry shrank to almost nothing. “I never would have expected A.I. could do this,” Mr. Bundi said.

His fate is shared by others who had found a foothold in the global online gig economy. Kenyans also transcribed meetings through the freelance platforms Upwork and Fiverr. They flagged Facebook posts to help the platform decide what could stay up. One after another, those opportunities have withered.

As technologists, economists and policymakers worldwide debate the future of A.I., Kenya’s experience shows how the technology is already dismantling some lower rungs of the global labor market.

“It’s not just going to be Kenya — it’s going to be everywhere we see a big transformation,” said Mark Graham, an Oxford University professor who has studied the global gig economy. “A.I. has come in and taken big chunks of these labor markets.”

Mr. Bundi said he had regrets. When he graduated from college in 2015, he bypassed a public health career to start an online essay-writing business, charging $40 to $70 per paper. Assignments came in through digital platforms, and he divvied up work between himself and students he hired. He rented a house near a university and filled it with desks, fast internet and mattresses. Students worked between classes and slept when too exhausted to write.

Mr. Bundi said he had made at least five times as much as he could earn in public health. He sent money to his parents, coffee farmers who had taken out a loan to buy him a laptop for college.

He sometimes considered the ethics of helping students cheat, but decided it was ultimately their choice. He said he saw himself as a tutor and was proud that a young Kenyan was thriving unnoticed inside Western academia.

Around Nairobi, new money among essay writers was visible. At its peak early this decade, at least 40,000 people in the city were being paid to do other people’s homework, researchers estimated. Essay writers drove new Subarus, carried the latest smartphones and booked exclusive tables at clubs.

After the crash, Mr. Bundi closed his essay-writing business and struggled to find a career path. He is now working for a German government development organization helping young Kenyans find opportunities in the digital economy. He said his experience was a cautionary tale.

“A.I. is coming for bankers, for accountants, it’s coming for engineers, and A.I. will come for architects,” he said. “It’s coming for everybody.”

Few have much sympathy for those aiding an international cheating scheme. But the “essay mills” were, in their way, a Kenyan success story.

More than 100,000 students graduate from Kenyan universities each year into an economy where salaried jobs are scarce. Roughly 80 percent of work is informal — delivery driving, construction, street vending — and youth unemployment is estimated to be over 25 percent. Lack of economic opportunity has fueled a Gen Z-led protest movement.

For a generation with degrees and nowhere to use them, gig work looked like the way out. Kenya’s government thought so, too.

After cheap high-speed internet began arriving around 2009, the government saw online outsourcing — transcription, data entry, graphic design, website development and basic software coding — as a way to climb the economic ladder. Essay writing, while never officially condoned, fit the model.

In 2016, the Kenyan government started a program training university graduates to navigate online freelancer platforms like Upwork. In 2022, the year ChatGPT appeared, Kenya adopted a 10-year National Digital Masterplan that further emphasized outsourcing and online gig work.

“We just wanted jobs,” said Frida Mwangi, 46, who in 2015 turned to transcription work as a path back to the work force while raising four children.

Gig work meant that she could show her daughter that a woman can be a mother and earn a living, Ms. Mwangi said. One big assignment was transcribing interviews of Ellis Island immigrants; she also did medical transcriptions.

That work began drying up in 2017 when transcription software became one of the earliest applications of A.I. Ms. Mwangi’s wages fell, and employers told her to use A.I. and supplement it with her own expertise. She found that process more time-consuming than transcribing on her own, because the A.I. butchered the medical terms. Still, the jobs disappeared.

“My job went completely,” said Ms. Mwangi, who now advocates for better pay and working conditions for gig workers.

Kenya’s outsourcing push brought jobs, but also a backlash. Firms hired by American tech giants faced criticism for low pay and poor working conditions.

That led to a pullback. Sama, a company that hired Kenyans to police user-generated content for Meta, cut back in the country. Scale AI, a start-up that hires people to train A.I. models, discontinued some Kenyan operations.

A.I.’s abilities continue to advance. One test from Scale AI and the Center for A.I. Safety tries to quantify A.I.’s ability to do online freelance work like product design and data analysis. Last October, leading A.I. models completed 2.5 percent of the tasks. By July, they completed 16 percent.

Many who grew up doing essay writing and other gig work are now struggling to find a way back into the labor force.

Alex Munyua, 30, an industrial chemist who worked in the essay business because it was more lucrative, briefly performed data labeling and social media moderation after the industry declined. Now that work has also gone.

“Some have gone back to the villages,” he said. “There are those that tried other sectors, but they were frustrated because they couldn’t get formal jobs.”

Kenya is being buffeted by economic turbulence, with 40 percent of its more than 54 million people living in poverty. Tech jobs are scarce, despite a start-up scene.

Richard Eshilache, 38, built a profitable career in essay writing and said he employed more than 100 writers in 2022. He worked for some overseas students so long that one sent him his diploma.

“He told me it is for the two of us,” Mr. Eshilache said.

He is now trying to embrace A.I. for jobs editing photos and data annotation. None of it pays as well as essay writing.

John Tanui, principal secretary in the Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, stood by Kenya’s economic potential as an outsourcing hub, saying it would “unlock opportunities for our young people.”

Yet what jobs remain in essay writing are mainly for “humanizers,” who edit papers written by A.I. to avoid detection from the cheating software used by many universities.

Alphline, who began essay writing in 2021 and gave only her first name for fear of harming future job prospects, said business was as good as ever. With A.I., she can do more work, using the technology to quickly write a first draft and then writing through it herself. She eschews A.I. tools designed to disguise A.I. writing as human, preferring her own touch.

“I can clearly tell a paper that’s A.I. generated compared to one that’s human generated,” she said. “But for a student that doesn’t have that human writing experience, they can get caught.”

For Mr. Bundi, the transition has been difficult. He said he missed the intellectual wrestling match of learning new subjects and writing under a tight deadline, as well as working with some students from when they were freshmen through graduate school.

“It was like getting a parallel education,” he said.

Mr. Bundi sometimes wonders what his life would have been like if he had stayed in public health.

“All my peers that started in 2015 after graduation, they rose through the ranks,” he said. “Now if I go back, I’ll start at an entry level working for somebody who graduated just last year.”

I first heard about Kenya’s essay-writing industry during Covid, when many stuck-at-home students outsourced their homework to people living across the world. Academics lamented the unethical behavior, but it also struck me as fascinating for what it said about globalization and the internet.

It was hard not to have some admiration for the smart young people making some money by doing the hard work that students in the United States, Britain and other English-speaking countries didn’t want to do. As artificial intelligence use exploded, making cheating even easier, my colleague Paul and I wondered about its impact on those writers and other online gig workers. On a recent reporting trip to Kenya, we sat down with several of them.

Edwin Okoth contributed reporting from Nairobi.

item.title: Scenic Route
item.description:
It’s Labor Day weekend, and I’m here to remind you that summer’s not over, even though schools and scolds try to lop off the final two weeks, declaring a premature finish to a season that, as any equinoctial will tell you, extends until Sept. 22. Hang on. Linger in the post-7 p.m. sunsets while you can. Finish the book you started in August. Make it to the beach. Stay a little looser. The apples and sweaters and soups are standing patiently by.

I’m reluctant to let summer go because I’m reluctant to button up, to start rushing again. I associate summer with wandering, both literally and culturally. I was chatting recently with my colleague Minju about this season’s big films — “Spider-Man,” “The Odyssey,” “The Devil Wears Prada 2” — and we realized our most satisfying cinematic experiences were the detours those blockbusters sent us on. Minju was reminded how much she likes Samantha Morton, who played Circe in “The Odyssey,” which sent her to rewatch other films Morton starred in, like “Jesus’ Son” and “Minority Report.”

I loved “The Invite,” directed by and starring Olivia Wilde, and set off to watch her in Gregg Araki’s “I Want Your Sex” from July, and also to revisit her prior directorial efforts, “Don’t Worry Darling” and “Booksmart.” “Don’t Worry Darling” stars Harry Styles, who’s currently performing a 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden. I didn’t get tickets, but I’ve been dancing to his delightful 2022 album “Harry’s House” all summer.

Of course the omnivorous consumer follows her aesthetic bliss year round, but the expansive days of the warmer months lend themselves to cultural meandering.

Minju read Rachel Cusk’s new book “Life of M,” then wandered back to her earlier “Outline” trilogy, which she’d meant to read but never had. Olivia Rodrigo’s duet with Robert Smith on her new album led me back to Smith’s days with the Cure, “Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Kiss Me” and other albums from the 1980s.

I had been eagerly anticipating “Remake,” Ross McElwee’s documentary about making art after the loss of his son. Before watching it, I went back to revisit his 1986 film, “Sherman’s March,” knowing the new one referenced it and I’d want to have it fresh in my mind. After seeing “Remake,” which was stunning, I immediately cued up McElwee’s 2011 doc about his son, “Photographic Memory,” and set out to find out where his other family documentaries were streaming. My McElwee journey was long, winding and totally absorbing, a cinematic ramble.

I like the wisdom to always be planning your next trip or vacation, even if it’s far in the future, so you have something to look forward to. If the end of summer brings with it a little sadness, as it does for me, why not plan your cultural itinerary for the fall? Where will “Practical Magic 2,” a 28-years-later sequel starring Sandra Bullock, Nicole Kidman and Dianne Wiest, lead? To Bullock’s hilarious turn in “The Heat”? Wiest in “Edward Scissorhands” or perhaps off the path to her small role in “Footloose”? Barbara Kingsolver’s new novel “Partita” comes out Oct. 6. Will we be rereading “The Poisonwood Bible” and “Demon Copperhead” come Halloween?

The origin is the equinox, the destination is the solstice. You can choose your waypoints, but the detours and diversions will emerge once you’re on the road.

Lindsay Clancy Trial

The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case declared a mistrial, after the jury failed to reach a verdict over several days of deliberations.

Clancy, who strangled her three children during what the defense called an episode of postpartum psychosis, will likely remain institutionalized as prosecutors decide whether to take the case to trial again.

The foreperson told the judge that there was a lone holdout in the jury who had expressed doubt about Clancy’s guilt but would not vote to acquit her.

Economy

Hiring was unexpectedly strong in August, as employers pushed past uncertainty related to the war in Iran, tariffs and A.I.

President Trump threatened to halt a broad swath of U.S. trade unless the Federal Reserve slashed interest rates.

Elections

The Homeland Security secretary asked the Justice Department to investigate a commonly used voting machine, in what appeared to be an effort to cast doubt on digital voting systems.

item.title: Following Stolen Cars From Canada to Russia
item.description:
Our new Canada-based investigative reporter, Jane Bradley, kicked off her tenure with a major story: tracking stolen cars from Canada across countries to learn where those vehicles end up. She teamed up with a London-based correspondent, Michael Schwirtz, on the six-month investigation, and this week Jane sat down to talk about how they got the story.

What first drew you guys to Canada’s car theft epidemic?

Our investigation began with a tip from a source at Interpol, the international police organization. The official had been tracking stolen cars across the world and noticed something surprising: Thousands of stolen Canadian cars were turning up in Russia. That had never been reported before, so my colleague Michael Schwirtz and I were immediately interested.

Where did you guys start, in terms of the reporting?

We had to understand just how big a black market this was for car thieves. We knew we needed records, and after months of speaking with sources at Interpol and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, we got them. They showed that Interpol had received nearly 5,000 reports of stolen Canadian cars found in Russia between February 2024 and July 2026. That made it by far the biggest overseas destination for Canada’s stolen cars.

Then we had to follow the entire smuggling route, from cars being stolen in Toronto neighborhoods, through Canadian ports like Montreal, to the United Arab Emirates, and from there to Russia. We spoke to law enforcement officials across Canada and Europe, from the Canada Border Services Agency and Mounties, to police officials across Interpol, Britain and Sweden.

This narrative unfolds in almost real time, as if you’re uncovering it as it’s happening. Is that how it felt during the reporting?

Reporting it felt more like a complicated puzzle, to be honest. We would get one piece — interviews with important police officials and the exclusive Interpol data, for example — but we still needed to figure out how those stolen cars got to Russia. That meant getting Canadian cops to talk to me and, when it became apparent how key the ports are in the car theft trade, persuading Canada’s Border Services Agency to give us access to a port operation to help us understand how these thieves physically smuggle the cars from Canada to Russia. That gave us the narrative.

What was your big breakthrough?

We had a couple. The first was obtaining the Interpol records showing the flow of stolen vehicles from Canada to Russia. It’s not publicly available, and it shone a light on an illicit trade that had been going on for years.

The second was when Michael persuaded a notorious Russian auto theft criminal known as the Wasp Killer to give him an interview from a prison in Ukraine. His real name is Daniil Aleynik, and he was in prison charged with involvement in an international car theft ring. We couldn’t quite believe it when he agreed to speak on the record about how the illicit trade worked and why Canada was such a target.

What surprised you about this story?

I was struck by how organized and sophisticated the trade is. These cars are stolen to order, and transnational organized criminal networks work together to meet a black market demand for expensive Western trucks and cars. Canadian investigators and Mr. Aleynik both described how orders would be placed in Russia — let’s say, for 15 Land Rovers — and this would be passed to scouts in Canada who worked scouring neighborhoods and parking lots for them.

Also surprising are the sophisticated tactics used by thieves to steal cars — for example, distracting drivers in parking lots to clone electronic fobs and using AirTags to track a car from shopping malls to homes that are easier to steal from at night.

Are the police adapting to fight car thefts?

The Canadian authorities have invested tens of millions of dollars into this. Other countries, such as Britain, are now looking to them for guidance on their own car theft problems. But tens of thousands of cars are still being stolen across Canada every year, thousands of which we know are smuggled overseas. Auto theft criminals like Mr. Aleynik are dismissive of Western efforts to crack down on the crime. He gave us this great quote: “In Russia, no one steals cars, because if you do, you won’t live long. In the West, a human life is worth more than a car.”

Jane Bradley is a Toronto-based investigative reporter covering Canada for The Times. Shawna Richer is The Times’s Canada editor. She lives in Toronto.

By Ian Austen

Thank you to everyone who took time to send in questions about the often baffling issues emerging from the tariffs that are now in place between Canada and the United States, as well as those of you who raised queries in comments on our articles.

Here are some answers to the questions you most commonly raised, and below, in case you missed it, our trade coverage from this week.

How has President Trump been able to impose tariffs after the United States Supreme Court declared them to be illegal? Doesn’t the power to introduce tariffs rest with Congress?

Congress has delegated its power over tariffs to presidents under certain circumstances through at least six laws. Last year, the Supreme Court ruled on Mr. Trump’s tariffs on more than 100 countries, including Canada, which were imposed under a 1970s emergency statute. The court ruled that the law did not allow Mr. Trump to impose tariffs unilaterally.

Those tariffs had very little effect on Canada. Anything shipped from Canada that qualified for free entry under what Canadians call the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement had continued to move along duty-free.

But that court ruling didn’t apply to the tariffs of up to 50 percent on steel, aluminum and autos that Mr. Trump also brought in last year. For those, Mr. Trump used a 1962 law that allows the president to place tariffs when the importing of products “threaten to impair the national security.”

While there are some current court challenges, legal experts told me that American judges generally defer to presidents on national security issues. But some of them said there is an argument that Mr. Trump did not clearly show how, for example, Canadian-made Toyotas endanger U.S. national security.

Finally, Mr. Trump dusted off a protectionist 1930 trade law — that many economists argue had made the Great Depression longer and more severe — for his latest 50 percent tariffs. The law has never been used. Any court actions are likely to argue that it was replaced or superseded by subsequent legislation.

Are Canadian shoppers actually avoiding American products? American-owned stores in Canada seem as crowded as ever.

With the exception of cross-border travel, there is no hard data on the extent of “Buy Canadian” campaigns. With travel, however, the pattern is clear. The latest figures from Statistics Canada show that it was down 29 percent from July 2024.

An indication of interest in avoiding American products was the decision last month by Loblaw, which operates under a variety of names across the country, to backtrack and restore country of origin labels on produce in its stores in several provinces. (Provincial laws meant that they had never disappeared in Ontario and Quebec.) The removal prompted a social media backlash from shoppers.

In a survey of Canadian manufacturers commissioned for KPMG, the consulting firm, 47 percent of the respondents said that “Buy Canadian” had increased sales. Many of the companies in the survey, however, do not make things sold directly to consumers.

Some economists suggest that one difficulty for the strategy is a dearth of Canadian-made consumer products in many categories.

If Canada and the United States do finally get a deal, what are the chances that Mr. Trump honors it?

After pulling Canada’s negotiators back from Washington last month, Prime Minister Mark Carney said of the United States under Mr. Trump: “Sometimes, its signature is written in pencil.”

All of the Trump tariffs, of course, are flagrant violations of the trade deal he negotiated, and repeatedly praised, during his first term in office.

Several American readers asked how they can support Canadian businesses affected by U.S. tariffs.

I can’t find any reliable list of Canadian consumer products available in American shops. There are some brands, however, that do promote their Canadian roots that also do some or all of their manufacturing in Canada, notably Canada Goose, Arc’teryx sportswear and Moosehead beer, with wide distribution in the United States.

The 17-digit vehicle identification numbers on Canadian made cars always begins with 2. All Chrysler minivans and Dodge Charger muscle cars sold in the United States are made in Canada. Most Lexus RX and NX models at American dealers come from Canada, although a few are made in Japan. All of the other vehicles made and shipped from Canada are also produced in American factories. But supplies are very tight for most of those vehicles, particularly the Toyota RAV4 and the Honda CR-V, most likely making it impractical to request Canadian-made ones.

If you do buy directly from Canadian companies’ websites, don’t put them on the spot by asking that they undervalue your purchase on the customs declaration to reduce the tariff bill when it crosses the border. Aside from raising the possibility that the parcel will be seized, there can be serious legal consequences for the seller.

Ian Austen reports on Canada for The Times. A Windsor, Ontario, native now based in Ottawa, he has reported on the country for two decades. He can be reached at austen@nytimes.com.

item.title: A Glitz-Free Place Named for Trump? Welcome to the Golan Heights.
item.description:
Seven years ago, Israel announced with great fanfare the establishment of Trump Heights, a settlement named for the glitz-loving American president. Today, despite the name, the place is about as far from the Trump aesthetic as imaginable.

The community is home to about 27 families living in a tight cluster of spartan, prefabricated homes in the rugged north of the Israeli-controlled Golan Heights, a few miles from the volatile frontiers with Lebanon and Syria.

The location would not appeal to everyone, but for some residents, the location is kind of the point. Trump Heights sits in a remote corner of the strategic plateau, with commanding views across northern Israel.

Its birth followed President Trump’s decision in 2019 to formally recognize Israeli authority over the long-disputed Golan, which Israel seized from Syria in the 1967 Middle East war and later annexed.

The Trump proclamation, citing security imperatives, reversed decades of American policy and flouted international opinion, which broadly views Israel’s occupation and annexation of the area as illegal. (Colombia became the second country to recognize Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights last month.)

Syria has long demanded the return of the Israeli-controlled Golan Heights. In the chaotic aftermath of the ouster of the dictator Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Israeli forces pushed deeper into southern Syria. Israel now occupies territory beyond a buffer zone established under a Disengagement Agreement in 1974, citing a need to secure its frontier.

Within weeks of Mr. Trump’s announcement, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other dignitaries held a festive ceremony at the desolate site designated for Trump Heights and unveiled an outsize sign emblazoned with the settlement’s name in gold lettering, and framed in still more gold for good measure.

A year later, the Israeli government approved initial funding of 8 million shekels (then about $2.3 million) to establish a temporary encampment of mobile homes at Trump Heights, and the first residents moved in 10 months after that. Officials said it would eventually accommodate 300 families.

Given the name, it was perhaps inevitable that visiting reporters would occasionally use the settlement, with its mixed population of secular and religious Jews, as an informal barometer of Israeli feelings toward Mr. Trump. These tend to veer sharply, not unlike his Middle East policies.

The inhabitants of Trump Heights are weary of being asked about the man it was named for, and they say they spend little time discussing either him or politics. Some say they feel no connection to the name and would not be averse to it changing.

“There were already discussions about it from the start,” said Daniel Biber, 32, a writer and editor. His family was the first to move here, in April 2021, and his wife, Tzofit, is the director of Trump Heights, known as Ramat Trump in Hebrew.

Only three months before they arrived, he noted, a mob of Trump supporters had stormed the U.S. Capitol. “In the end,” Mr. Biber said, “he’s the president of the United States, not ours.”

In the eyes of many Israelis, Mr. Trump has lurched over the past year from being a national savior to an antihero.

First, he helped secure a deal with Hamas to bring Israeli hostages back from Gaza. Not long afterward, he joined Mr. Netanyahu in going to war against Iran, Israel’s archenemy. Then he made a preliminary deal with Tehran that even longtime Trump and Netanyahu supporters in Israel viewed as a dangerous gamble with their security, and curbed Israeli action against Hezbollah in Lebanon. Mr. Netanyahu recently rejected Mr. Trump’s plan for disarming Hamas in Gaza.

An opinion survey by the Israel Democracy Institute, an independent research group, indicated that Mr. Trump’s popularity was at a new low this summer, with only 28 percent of Israelis believing he prioritized their security, down from 64 percent in March.

Mr. Biber said the residents of Trump Heights spanned the spectrum when it came to Mr. Trump. Defining himself as a political centrist, Mr. Biber said Mr. Trump’s recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights was not a major consideration in his family’s decision to move there.

About 22,000 Israelis live in more than 30 settlements dotting the plateau, alongside a similar number of Druse residents in four main villages. The Druse, an Arabic-speaking religious minority spread across Lebanon, Syria and northern Israel, practice a faith often described as an offshoot of Ismaili Islam.

Several residents of Trump Heights said they came not out of ideology, but to live close to nature in a small, like-minded and tolerant Jewish community. Druse assistants work in the community’s kindergarten.

It is a far cry from Mar-a-Lago or Trump Tower. The only hint of gold here is on the faded sign at the entrance — a local attraction, with Israelis coming to take selfies with it as a backdrop. (Before the U.S. election in 2024, a group of ultra-Orthodox Jews came to light candles and pray for Mr. Trump to win.)

The grounds are sunbaked and thorny, and an old sign on a section of chain link perimeter fence warns of land mines. There was an earlier attempt, 35 years ago, to establish a community here, for immigrants from the former Soviet Union. Most abandoned the place, for lack of a livelihood, though a handful remained.

For now, Trump Heights offers a simple life with a small library, a modest synagogue and a used clothing store. Families won plots for permanent homes through a lottery. They get the land for free, but said it would most likely take years and more than $650,000 to build an average house.

The population is overwhelmingly young, with 85 children under 13 and more on the way. Many adults work remotely, and family dwellings are only about 600 square feet — roughly the size of a studio apartment.

Residents and future homeowners marked five years of community life with a potluck meal and activities for the children.

They have thoughts about foreign policy but are much more engaged in the details of daily life.

Dotan Gal, 39, was with his two children in the hamlet’s small playground. Here, he said, the burning question was whether to get a new swing set. “The pace of this place doesn’t match with the pace of the news,” he said.

The nearest supermarket is at least a 20-minute drive away. A residents’ WhatsApp group is full of requests like “Who has milk?” or some pita bread.

Noa Aviad, 42, a mother of five young children, said she was afraid for the days after the Trump presidency, with sentiment in the United States becoming less sympathetic to Israel.

Her youngest child, Matan Shalom, was born last October, two years after the Hamas-led attack on Israel that set off the devastating war in Gaza. His name is a prayer for peace, Ms. Aviad said.

“People here feel — like many Israelis — that Trump doesn’t ‘get’ the region,” viewing everything in transactional business terms, she said.

Trump Heights can feel like a distant outpost far removed from the world’s problems — more like a social experiment for a country wracked by tensions between the religious and the secular, Jews and Arabs, conservatives and liberals.

The aim, Ms. Aviad said, is to build a Jewish community made up of equal numbers of religious couples, secular couples and mixed couples.

Its vision statement includes the “aspiration to become an example for connection” between the disparate parts of Israeli society.

The more heated discussions tend to revolve around subjects like the level of Orthodoxy adhered to in the synagogue and how strictly kosher the food needs to be at a potluck.

“Unlike in the city, where there is a choice, here we have to find solutions that satisfy as many people as possible and do the least harm,” said Amalia Grinvald Urbach, a religiously observant architect and a mother of five.

Asked what Mr. Trump might make of the place should he visit, Ms. Aviad, sitting in her yard strewed with toys, laundry and utensils, said it might need sprucing up a bit.

Mr. Biber, the writer, said the president would probably not want to stay long.

But his name seems likely to stay for the foreseeable future. “We learned to live with it,” Mr. Biber said. “One day he won’t be president, and we will remain here.”

item.title: English Museum to Repatriate Colonial-Era Human Remains
item.description:
After years of negotiations, a British museum has agreed to return a colonial-era collection of human remains to the Indigenous Naga people of the Indian subcontinent, Naga representatives said on Saturday.

The partial remains — a warrior’s cranium, a woman’s skull, a young person’s jaw and many others — have been far from home in the Pitt Rivers Museum at the University of Oxford for over 100 years.

They were included in an exhibit called “Treatment of Dead Enemies,” under the label “headhunting trophies,” displayed alongside remains from other Indigenous groups including the shrunken heads of the Shuar people of South America. That changed in 2020, when the museum took down 120 human remains, including those of the Naga, and put them in storage.

On Saturday, a Naga delegation announced that the 39 pieces of Naga remains would return to Nagaland, a small northeastern state in India, by the end of the year.

“We bring back the light of our ancestors that was dimmed but never extinguished,” said Ellen Konyak of the Forum for Naga Reconciliation in making the announcement. The nonprofit forum worked with the museum, which has the world’s largest collection of Naga cultural objects, and Naga tribal groups on the repatriation effort.

A “monument of healing and peace” symbolizing Naga unity will be built at their resting place, the forum said.

Laura Van Broekhoven, the director at Pitt Rivers, said the handover, scheduled for November, will be the largest repatriation of human remains from the museum. She called the process a “Naga-wide movement of healing and unification.”

Representatives of the Naga have sought the remains for years. Formal discussions with the Pitt Rivers Museum began in 2020.

“It is a celebration,” Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist and professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz, said in an interview before the announcement. “It is the homecoming of our loved ones. A group of our elders are returning.” She, along with Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology at the University of Edinburgh, initiated the repatriation process.

Most of the Naga remains in the Pitt Rivers Museum were donated by J.P. Mills and J.H. Hutton, British officers who were posted in the Naga regions of British India during the early 1900s. While some of these were given by Naga as gifts, most were collected under duress and often against the wishes of the Naga people, anthropologists said.

The ancestral remains in Britain came to symbolize the Naga people’s struggle, many of those involved with the repatriation said. That history includes the efforts of American Christian missionaries in the 19th century that eroded traditional Naga beliefs and practices, and decades of conflict with the Indian state after independence from Britain, when many Nagas resisted becoming a part of the new country.

“Every Naga is talking about the human remains,” said Longyang Chang, a 28-year-old artist based in Kohima, the capital of Nagaland, whose work recently featured in an exhibition that explored how Naga cultural objects had been used as “dehumanized exotic artifacts.” The exhibition grew out of conversations around the repatriations, said one of its curators, Throngkiuba Yimchungru.

In talking about who these people were and why their remains were taken away and put on display, “the Nagas were revisiting their traumatic past and reconciling with it,” Mr. Chang said.

Large collections of Naga ancestral remains are still held by other universities and museums across Europe and the United States and by private collectors. In October 2024, a Naga skull was offered at auction for a starting price of 3,500 British pounds, about $4,700 at current exchange rates, at an event titled “The Curious Collector Sale.” The sale was halted after an outcry from Naga community members.

“It is my desire to see such trade being deemed illegal in the U.K.,” Ms. Kikon said.

A delegation of 20 Naga leaders and scholars visited the Pitt Rivers Museum in June last year to see the remains stored there for the first time. “I was shocked to see the skulls,” said the Rev. A. Peihwang Wangsa, who was part of the group.

“I was so angry,” he said. “I could not understand how they were used like this for so long.”

Before leaving, the Naga delegation placed several traditional shawls with the remains, each representing a Naga tribe. The shawls restored the ancestors’ connections to their Naga communities, the group said.

“The shawls,” Mr. Wangsa said, “have finally led our ancestors home.”

item.title: Here Is Where Ukraine Peace Talks Stand, as a New Round Approaches
item.description:
Trump administration envoys arrived on Saturday in Moscow in an effort to restart talks to end the war between Russia and Ukraine, over six months after a previous round of discussions fizzled out.

The trip by Steve Witkoff, the administration’s peace envoy, and Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, came even as Russian and Ukrainian forces are locked in an escalating spiral of airstrikes.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said on Thursday that U.S. envoys would “have a meeting in Moscow and another one in Kyiv,” Ukraine’s capital. He added: “It is important that America remain actively engaged. We are ready to meet with them in Ukraine — properly and substantively.”

Kyrylo Budanov, the Ukrainian delegation’s leader at the previous talks, told The New York Times in a recent interview that negotiations mediated by the Trump administration were expected to begin by late September, days after Russia’s parliamentary election and weeks before U.S. midterm elections.

It is not clear whether a new round of talks will yield more progress than previous ones. But “negotiations will sooner or later come to something,” Mr. Budanov told The Times. “You cannot fight your whole life.”

Here is what to know about peace talks and where they stand.

Russia and Ukraine have been talking at various levels since February 2022, when Russian forces mounted a full-scale invasion of Ukrainian territory. Despite brief cease-fires and occasional prisoner swaps, the two sides have made little headway toward ending the war.

A new flurry of high-level, U.S.-brokered negotiations began shortly after Mr. Trump — who claimed he could end the war in a day — took office in January 2025.

The last round of face-to-face talks was held in February, when Ukrainian and Russian negotiators met in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, and then later in Geneva. But there was no breakthrough in those discussions, and they ground to a halt after the United States and Israel went to war against Iran, a conflict that has consumed the Trump administration’s attention.

Since then, there have been limited contacts between Moscow and Kyiv, but the major issues have remained on hold.

In June, Mr. Zelensky published an open letter to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia that offered to resume peace talks, but that also taunted the Russian leader. Mr. Putin, who has shown little serious interest in peace negotiations, recently pledged to pursue the war.

The last round of negotiations focused a 20-point peace plan that covered a broad range of issues, including security guarantees that Ukraine seeks to prevent future Russian aggression, and commitments to rebuild the war-ravaged nation.

But the two sides have struggled to reach common ground on several crucial points, including the possible deployment of Western forces in Ukraine, control of territory in the country’s east, and management of a Russian-occupied nuclear power plant.

Russia has demanded that Ukraine hand over the land it controls in the eastern Donetsk region as a condition for ending the war, a strip of territory about 50 miles long and 40 miles wide that includes dozens of towns and villages. Ukraine has refused to withdraw unilaterally, arguing that ceding land would embolden Russia to attack again, and it has asked for guarantees that would deter Moscow from violating any cease-fire.

The United States has been the main mediator in talks between Russia and Ukraine.

But European leaders — nervous that Mr. Trump will cut them out of any settlement — are trying to take a more active role in ending the war, whose outcome could shape the continent’s security for decades to come. Mr. Trump has also made it clear that he sees Ukraine as a European responsibility.

European diplomats are working on a format for future negotiations to protect European interests that would be led by France, Germany and Britain, European officials said last month.

The front, stretching hundreds of miles through eastern Ukraine, has largely been frozen. The terrain has been devastated, a killing field dominated by drones, making troop movement a lethal risk.

As a result, Russia and Ukraine have instead intensified a campaign of airstrikes that have caused death and destruction in cities far from the battlefield. Over the summer, the two sides have launched drones and missiles at energy infrastructure, commercial warehouses and ports that are crucial to grain exports.

Russia has pummeled Kyiv with unrelenting daytime attacks of new jet-powered drones, taking advantage of a Ukrainian shortage of air defenses. Ukraine has launched attacks increasingly deep into Russia’s territory, disrupting its economy and isolating Crimea.

Even if negotiations resume this month, conditions for a cease-fire are unlikely to come until spring, Mr. Budanov told The Times. Russia is expected to attempt to break Ukraine in another strategic winter bombing campaign, the fourth of the war.

item.title: Flee, Hide or Sit Tight? Russians Are on Edge Over Rumors of a Draft.
item.description:
As anxiety over rumors of a forced military mobilization began to sweep through Moscow, Eradzh, a 36-year-old entrepreneur, turned to his A.I. assistant to parse the news and calculate the likelihood of a draft.

Eventually, the probability became high enough that he asked the program to find him a cheap flight out of Russia. In about a week, Eradzh will fly to Cyprus and spend at least two months away from Moscow.

Ticking off points on his fingers, Eradzh explained his logic as Russia has churned through tens of thousands of volunteer soldiers lured to the battlefield in Ukraine through fat payouts, while making only small gains in territory.

“Have the contract soldiers most likely run out? They’ve run out,” he said. “Have we captured anything? We haven’t. Did the negotiations lead anywhere? They didn’t. Will Putin dig his heels in? He will dig his heels in.”

“Will there be a mobilization? Most likely, yes,” he said recently in a cafe in central Moscow. Eradzh, like others interviewed, agreed to talk only on the condition that his last name not be used.

For months, the fear of a possible mobilization — a second wave of the draft that began in September 2022 — has become a fixture of daily life across Russia.

Rumors that Moscow might force more people to fight in the war after a parliamentary election on Sept. 20 have filled online information spaces and are discussed in cafes, on trains and in smoking areas near offices.

The Kremlin has denied that any mobilization is being prepared. On Wednesday, President Vladimir V. Putin called the reports “complete nonsense” and an “information attack against Russia.” On Thursday, he doubled down on his denial, saying that Russia had enough troops and that “as of today, there is no scenario that would require a mobilization.”

As the rumors have swirled, the Russian authorities have tried to project calm. Moscow has remained as orderly and manicured as ever, with pavilions on its central boulevards offering free medical checkups under the slogan, “Your choice is to live longer!”

Still, many people are not convinced by the government’s assurances. They cite previous denials by the Kremlin that turned out not to be true, like the repeated ones in 2022 that Russia was not going to invade Ukraine or conduct a wave of mobilization that September.

Russians point to separate, so far isolated examples of more hard-line recent recruitment tactics reported in the Penza region, southeast of Moscow. They also note that Mr. Putin’s decree ordering the draft back in 2022 technically remains in force, and therefore a mobilization could happen stealthily.

Fears have been fueled by international media reports citing Western intelligence officials, who say that Russia is losing more troops than it recruits, and statements from Ukraine’s leaders. In August, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said that Russia planned to draft 300,000 people after the parliamentary election. Mr. Zelensky made similar a prediction in April 2024.

When Russia conducted its first large forced mobilization in 2022, hundreds of thousands of men fled Russia. The draft shook Russian society to such an extent that officials scrambled to halt it within weeks.

That mobilization was intended to shore up a Russian Army that was on the brink of collapse in Ukraine, military analysts said. Outnumbered, Moscow’s forces abandoned large swaths of occupied land in Ukraine’s east and south, leaving their equipment behind.

Russia’s current situation on the front line is nowhere near what it was in fall 2022, said Dmitri Kuznets, a military analyst.

Mr. Kuznets said that, contrary to Western assessments, Russia was still recruiting more people than it lost on the battlefield, according to verifiable data from the Russian budget, notary databases and obituary notices. He also said that unlike in 2022, the Russian state lacked the money to pay conscripts in another large-scale draft wave.

“Theoretically, it could be used to create new units and formations,” Mr. Kuznets said, referring to a draft. But the potential gains would be outweighed by the risk of mass public anger at the Kremlin, he added.

Still, Mr. Kuznets said, Mr. Putin might not make a rational decision. And while Russia might not suffer from an acute shortage of personnel overall, it lacks specific types of servicemen — most of all nimble drone operators, he said.

In the end, perhaps only Mr. Putin knows whether there will be a mobilization. That has left ordinary Russians unsure what to do next.

Aleksandr, 36, a fitness coach in Moscow, said he had simply gotten tired of losing sleep and “endlessly wondering whether it’s going to happen or not.”

At the end of August, he flew to Thailand with his wife, who is also a fitness coach and who wept, he said, over losing her life in Russia. As a former serviceman in a special unit, he said, he faced too high a risk of being drafted.

Ivan, 24, a civil engineer, said he and his friends specifically planned their annual vacation abroad to cover the period just before and after the parliamentary election. They will monitor the news while hiking in Georgia, he said.

Ilya, 26, another engineer, said he had decided to leave after Yabloko, the only political party running on a pro-peace platform, was removed from the ballot. He also cited gasoline shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes and reports of increased harassment of travelers at the border as factors in his decision.

“You don’t know what the authorities might do to limit your movement and your efforts to keep yourself alive and well,” he said.

Others who would like to leave lack the means. Some said they were trying to get official residency in Moscow, which many believe will be shielded from a draft. Others have withdrawn money from their bank accounts, fearing that the funds could be frozen if they receive an online summons and fail to appear at an enlistment office.

Mikhail, 40, who works in the film industry, said that he had sought help from a psychiatrist after scrolling through so many reports about the possibility of mobilization.

“I’m trying to bring myself back from this field of rumors and speculation into something that I really know,” he said, “but actually I know nothing.”

Ilya, 31, who works in logistics, said he was not concerned about mobilization as such, but about the effect it could have on the Russian economy. It could halt already slow growth and force more companies to close because of a lack of personnel. “We would have to lay off people at work,” he said.

Many said that another wave of the draft would be much harder to escape than the one in 2022, after a digitization of the government’s conscription system.

Summonses to report to the military are now delivered electronically. Those who do not comply face automatic bans on leaving the country, as well as suspensions of driver’s licenses and the right to conduct property transactions.

The system of automated penalties is not yet fully working because of a lack of coordination between government agencies and technical difficulties, said Grigory Sverdlin, founder of Idite Lesom — meaning get lost in Russian — a group that helps Russians evade military conscription.

Konstantin, a yachting coach in St. Petersburg, said that while he had stayed away from Russia during the first wave of mobilization in 2022, this time he planned to sit tight.

“During that first draft, a lot of my friends made drastic moves — spending heaps of money, trying to get citizenship elsewhere, things like that,” he said. “But eventually, they all came back.”

Alina Lobzina contributed reporting.

item.title: After Months at War, Brief Solace in a Party Town Far From Home
item.description:
After 286 days at sea, the sailors and Marines of the warship Abraham Lincoln savored the pleasures of Pattaya, Thailand. Their indulgences were not all decadent.

They ate Double Super Cheeseburgers at Burger King. They shopped for LeBron James jerseys at the mall. They sipped from fresh coconuts at the beach, their backs to the water where they had spent the last nine-plus months.

And they danced with scantily clad women at nightclubs, the pounding music seemingly even louder than the aural assault of an aircraft carrier at war.

Pattaya is used to welcoming American servicemen. The beach town grew from an R&R refuge for American military personnel during the Vietnam War. For five days beginning on Wednesday, its pool halls, steakhouses and spas, its go-go bars, burrito shacks and trinket stalls have turned their attention to the 5,000 or so service members from the Lincoln, one of four carriers used in the air campaign against Iran.

100 miles

MYANMAR

LAOS

THAILAND

Bangkok

CAMBODIA

Pattaya

Andaman

Sea

Gulf of

Thailand

The New York Times

After a grueling deployment that fed criticism of the Trump administration’s execution of the war, the service members aboard the Lincoln had been instructed not to speak with members of the news media during their time in Pattaya.

Nevertheless, seven sailors confirmed, on the condition of anonymity, that the carrier’s long months at sea, especially without any of the normal stops at so-called liberty ports, had sapped both supplies and morale. They spoke of clogged toilets and, alarmingly, of multiple suicide attempts. (Navy officials have denied an increase in suicide attempts on the Lincoln.) Amid Iranian missile barrages and drone attacks, the half-day shifts merged into a Sisyphean blur, without the usual relief of care packages from home or treats from the ship store.

Meals were rationed, they said, and offered up a monotony of carbs. What she was really craving, one sailor said, was a salad, something green and fresh. Was there one to be had in Pattaya? There was.

The worst, a sailor from Illinois said, was not knowing how much longer they would be at sea. He stopped counting the days at around 200, despairing that the deployment might never end. Another sailor, a New York native, said that he had gone through a dozen deployments without incident, but this time he had watched junior sailors break, one by one. The price of war, he said, was something he was willing to bear, but not when a logistical crisis, which left the carrier with dwindling supplies, seemed preventable.

Did they, he continued — not defining the “they” — think for a moment about the mental health of those aboard the Lincoln? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said that reports of difficult conditions aboard the Lincoln were “misrepresented.” President Trump opined that the Lincoln’s deployment was “not nearly long enough.”

The residents of Pattaya, at least, appeared to understand the hardship borne by the crew of the Lincoln, which will head next toward its home port, San Diego. Pattaya’s mayor turned up to greet the men and women touching dry land for the first time since November. A gem shop offered discounts to the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps personnel. The Sapphire Club, an adult entertainment venue, dispatched three women in strapless black bodysuits to hold placards offering discounts for those with valid U.S. military ID.

At the Tahitian Queen, which bills itself as the oldest bar in Pattaya, circa 1978, Mickey Foth, one of the owners and an American military veteran and former Pentagon employee, teared up as he considered the sacrifices made by the Lincoln’s personnel.

“It’s not just the physical stress, it’s the emotional toll of such a long deployment,” he said, as a line of women in bikinis, one in an American flag pattern, gyrated onstage. “I want to be here, front and center, to say to these men and women, ‘Thank you for your service.’”

On Thursday night, some of the young sailors blushed amid the sexual maelstrom of Pattaya’s Walking Street, with its touts offering intricate shows involving improbably placed pingpong balls. Others, in the throbbing confines of nightclubs, downed shots and leaned close to female companions. Most of the women were Thai, some were Eastern European and Russian, a few were from neighboring countries like Myanmar and Laos or from as far away as Uganda and Uzbekistan.

Prostitution is illegal in Thailand, but you wouldn’t know it in Pattaya. Ever since American bombing missions took off from a nearby Thai air base during the Vietnam War, the village of Pattaya rapidly expanded its red-light district. Business boomed. With the arrival of the Lincoln, local entrepreneurs talked up the positive effect on Pattaya’s economy.

In earlier decades, some women and girls from Thailand’s poor northeast were sold by their families into sex work in Pattaya. While local aid groups say such human trafficking has waned, the criminalization of prostitution, even as it is openly tolerated, can put prostitutes at the mercy of corrupt forces or periodic crackdowns. In the days leading up to the Lincoln’s docking at a nearby port, the police in Pattaya launched an anti-prostitution raid that, like many before it, seemed to have had little lingering effect, apart from stigmatizing the women.

Today, servicemen are a much smaller demographic in Pattaya, compared to tourists from India, China and the Middle East. Amid the sex shows and vendors selling tubes of personal lubricant, vacationing families toted sleeping children, taking in the scene.

“Pattaya has been able to develop itself as a tourist destination, not only for sex tourism but also for culture, temples, family,” said Chanan Yodhong, a gender and sexual equality activist.

On Thursday night, as some sailors and Marines strolled or sat on the curb reeling from too much to drink, a corps of tourist police stood at attention before scattering into the crowds. There were also volunteer officers, residents who are originally from other parts of Asia, Europe and the Middle East.

Among them was Hooman Peseshk, a native of Iran, who has lived in Pattaya for 10 years. He recognized the irony of his patrolling the streets with a shipful of American sailors returning from the war in Iran. But he loved Pattaya, he said, for its status as a free port, where almost anything goes.

“Nobody wants to fight in a war that was started because of our leaders,” he said. “We are all brothers here in Pattaya.”

Despite the beach town’s reputation, many others from the Lincoln said they had no interest in exploring Play Girlz, KINK or the Harem Ultra go-go club. Instead, they dined poolside at the Hilton. They tried out foot spas where little fish nibbled off calluses. At the Hard Rock Hotel, where the minibar comes stocked with chocolate- and strawberry- flavored condoms, a member of the Lincoln crew said he was planning to spend the night ordering room service for one and watching sports on the big-screen TV.

One sailor said that after so many months aboard the carrier — with its frantic sirens, clattering pipes, screaming jet engines, explosive catapult launches — what he missed most was silence. Pattaya is many things, but it is not quiet. For that the sailor would have to wait.

John Ismay contributed reporting from Washington.
